description: We are Phantom Lynxes, a team united by a passion for spaceflight. For our first NASA Space Apps Challenge, we chose astronaut health monitoring, a problem that sits right at the intersection of software engineering and human physiology. Driven by our combined background across physics, data, design, coding and software, we built an approach directly grounded in the NASA Human Research Program's core framework on the five hazards of spaceflight.
summary: TotusGear is a crew health decision-support prototype that brings together conditions inside the habitat, possible changes inside the astronaut, and radiation protection. Its TEFC sensor module records cabin temperature, pressure, acceleration, and MQ-135 gas-sensor voltage, flagging sudden changes and sustained deviations. Phantom, our BioGears-based forecasting layer, projects measures such as pulse, blood pressure, blood volume, and urine output about two hours ahead using simulated physiology. CRAD uses radiation simulations to explore how shielding can be placed around sensitive organs within a limited mass budget. By showing measured data, simulated forecasts, and modeled protection together—and clearly distinguishing among them, TotusGear helps crews see what has changed and decide what to check next. The sensor module is a physical prototype; the physiological forecasts and CRAD design still require validation before operational use.
details:
TotusGear is a crew health decision-support prototype that helps astronauts connect conditions in their habitat with possible effects on their health. It brings together three components: TEFC, which measures the cabin environment; Phantom, which forecasts selected physiological measures using BioGears simulations; and CRAD, which investigates radiation shielding around sensitive organs. The interface distinguishes measured readings from simulated forecasts and modeled protection estimates, so a crew member can see what has changed and decide what to check next.

TEFC uses an ESP32 sensor unit in a 3D-printed enclosure. It records time-stamped temperature, pressure, three-axis acceleration, and MQ-135 air-quality sensor voltage to a local CSV file, with data also exported for viewing in Google Sheets then a later port to project site. Its rules flag sudden changes and sustained deviations. Phantom uses BioGears 8.2.0 simulation outputs to project pulse, mean arterial pressure, blood volume, and urine output approximately two hours ahead. In one held-out simulation, the team reported reducing pulse prediction error from 7.0 to 0.8 beats per minute. CRAD uses Geant4 radiation simulations to explore how UHMWPE shielding could be distributed according to organ sensitivity and protection gained per unit of mass.

We developed the project with ESP32 hardware, environmental and motion sensors, a 3D-printed case, Arduino IDE firmware, Python-based analysis and interface code, CSV data, BioGears, and Geant4. NASA research and bed-rest analog data helped inform our understanding of spaceflight health risks and reference behavior.

Our creative approach is to put the habitat, the body, and protection into one crew-facing workflow. The intended benefit is earlier recognition of concerning trends and clearer decisions about which measurement or inspection to perform next, especially when communication with Earth is delayed. We considered sensor calibration, false alerts, limited onboard resources, shielding mass, and the difference between a prediction and a verified health measurement. The current physiology results come from simulations, CRAD remains a modeled design, and a proposed network of TEFC units for locating cabin problems still requires testing. TotusGear is intended to support crew judgment, not provide an autonomous medical diagnosis.
